title: Convert a list of CSV lines ("name,department,salary") into a `List<Employee>` by splitting each line and constructing objects inside `map()`.
shortTitle: Convert a list of CSV lines ("name,department,salary") into a List<Employee> by splitting each line and constructing objects inside map()

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a parsing `map` that transforms each raw CSV string into a structured domain object. Inside the mapping function you split the line on the delimiter, trim and parse each token to its correct type, and construct the `Employee`, so the stream goes from `Stream<String>` to `Stream<Employee>`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The data-entry clerk at the National Bank of India receives a plain text file where each line is "Rajesh,IT,95000". She reads each line, chops it at the commas, and fills in a proper employee form with the pieces. `map` doing the split-and-construct is exactly that turning of a raw line into a filled form.

**One line to remember:** `map` can parse each raw line by splitting it and constructing a typed object from the pieces.

sections.s2_technical:
The mapping function receives a CSV line and must produce an Employee. First it splits the line with `line.split(",")`, which returns a String array of tokens. For the format name comma department comma salary, index zero is the name, index one is the department, and index two is the salary text that still needs converting to a number.

Because salary is money, you parse it into a `BigDecimal`, never a double. `new BigDecimal(parts[2].trim())` converts the text exactly. Trimming each token is important because CSV data often has stray spaces after commas, and an untrimmed " 95000" or a department with a leading space would corrupt the value or the parse.

Defensive parsing matters in a bank. A malformed line with too few fields would throw an array index out of bounds, and a non-numeric salary would throw a number format exception. In production you either validate each line and skip or route bad rows to an error list, or you let a strict parser fail loudly so corrupt data never silently enters the system. For the core demonstration the map constructs the object; a robust version wraps the parse and filters out lines that fail.

A senior nuance: naive splitting on comma breaks if a field itself contains a comma, for example a department written as "Sales, North". Real CSV uses quoting rules, so for anything beyond trivial input a proper CSV library such as OpenCSV or Apache Commons CSV is the correct choice rather than a hand-rolled split.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a nightly batch file from an external HR vendor where each employee is one plain line like "Rajesh,IT,95000". Before the data is usable it must become proper Employee objects with a real BigDecimal salary. This is exactly how a parsing map works — each line is split at the commas, each piece is trimmed and converted to the right type, and a structured Employee is constructed.

The code defines an `Employee` with name, department and a `BigDecimal` salary. A `CsvImportService` exposes `parse(List<String>)` that maps each line by splitting and constructing. The runnable `Main` feeds sample CSV lines and logs the constructed employees.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three CSV lines, one with stray spaces: "Rajesh,IT,95000", "Priya, Sales, 72000", "Amit,HR,48000".

Step 1: The stream opens over three raw strings.

Step 2: The first line enters map. split at commas gives the array Rajesh, IT, 95000. Each token is trimmed, salary text 95000 becomes a BigDecimal, and a new Employee is constructed.

Step 3: The second line, which has spaces after the commas, splits into "Priya", " Sales", " 72000". Trimming removes the leading spaces, so the department becomes Sales and the salary parses cleanly to 72000 — this shows why trimming matters.

Step 4: The third line parses to Amit, HR, 48000.

Step 5: The stream's element type is now Employee, not String, with three elements because map is one-to-one.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the three constructed Employee objects into a list.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Stream<String> ["Rajesh,IT,95000", "Priya, Sales, 72000", "Amit,HR,48000"]
    │
    ▼
  map(line -> parse)
    ├─ "Rajesh,IT,95000"    → split → [Rajesh|IT|95000] → new Employee(..., BigDecimal)
    ├─ "Priya, Sales, 72000"→ split → trim → [Priya|Sales|72000] → new Employee
    └─ "Amit,HR,48000"      → split → [Amit|HR|48000] → new Employee
    │  (type String → Employee, one-to-one)
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  List<Employee> (structured, BigDecimal salaries)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To turn raw CSV lines into structured objects I use a parsing map, where the mapping function splits each line on the comma, trims every token, converts each piece to its proper type, and constructs the domain object. Each line yields exactly one Employee, so the stream goes from a stream of strings to a stream of employees, which I collect into a list.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was the nightly import from an external HR vendor, where every employee arrived as one plain line like Rajesh comma IT comma ninety-five thousand. The crucial detail was parsing the salary into a BigDecimal rather than a double, because it is money, and trimming every token, because the vendor's file often had stray spaces after the commas that would otherwise corrupt a department name or break the number parse.

A senior point I always raise is defensive parsing and the limits of naive splitting. A malformed line with too few fields throws an array index exception, and a non-numeric salary throws a number format exception, so in production I validate each line and either skip bad rows into an error list or fail loudly, so corrupt data never silently enters the bank's systems. I also note that splitting on a plain comma breaks the moment a field itself contains a comma, like a department written as Sales comma North, because real CSV uses quoting rules — so for anything beyond trivial input I reach for a proper CSV library such as OpenCSV rather than a hand-rolled split.
